abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by amyloid {beta} (A{beta}) deposition, tau aggregation and impaired proteostasis, including autophagy dysfunction. However, how autophagy deficiency affects A{beta} pathology and disease progression remains unclear. We crossed excitatory neuronspecific Atg7 knockout mice with App knock-in mice (AppNL-F/NL-F and AppNL-G-F/NL-G-F) and assessed A{beta} pathology, extracellular vesicle (EV) release, cognition, gamma oscillatory activity, cell death, brain atrophy and proteomic changes. Autophagy deficiency reduced extracellular A{beta} plaque burden despite increased release of A{beta}-containing EVs. Notably, combined Arctic-A{beta} pathology and autophagy deficiency impaired gamma oscillatory activity, behaviour and memory, activated cell death signalling and shortened lifespan. CA1 proteomics identified a voltage-gated potassium channel subunit markedly increased upon Atg7 deletion. Surprisingly, less pronounced A{beta} pathology counteracted several detrimental effects, potentially through improved cellular transport and reduced protein translation. These findings reveal that autophagy regulates A{beta} metabolism and that A{beta} pathology severity determines the consequences of autophagy deficiency, highlighting autophagy modulation as a context-dependent therapeutic target in AD.
